Judged locally: no network access, no browsing history uploaded. The shield in the address bar shows the current site\'s risk level in real time.
Beyond clear risks, unusual domains and suspicious suffixes also trigger a prompt. The strictest option.
Blocks only when fraud, impersonation or malware is confirmed. Balances safety and smoothness.
The shield still shows risk status but never blocks the page; you decide.

URL deception, domain impersonation, punycode, suspicious suffixes, raw IP addresses, abnormal domain structures, plus invalid certificates and mixed content. Everything runs locally; no requests are sent.
These permissions apply to web requests in real time: always allow or deny takes effect immediately; ask each time prompts you first.

When a site wants the microphone (e.g. voice search or input): always allow or deny takes effect immediately; ask each time shows a prompt and remembers your choice per site. Choosing Always deny also revokes the system recording permission (Android 13+, performed by the system at a suitable time; the app may restart then).

If ZexBrowse works well for you, consider buying the author a coffee.

ZexBrowse is maintained by an individual in their spare time. It stays free, has no ads, and is not listed on any app store. Your support goes toward ongoing development and maintenance, as well as test devices.
Sponsorship is entirely voluntary and any amount is welcome; not sponsoring does not affect any feature.
1. Tap Sponsorship below to open the project README.
2. Scroll up to find the donation QR image in the Sponsorship section.
3. Long-press to save it (or take a screenshot), then open WeChat Scan and pick it from your album.
Thank you for using ZexBrowse whether or not you sponsor. Feedback on the GitHub repository is always welcome.

Images and similar resources load over plain HTTP. Sign-in is unaffected, but content could be swapped.
This link hides the real site behind an "@": you would actually visit %1$s. This is a common phishing trick.
This domain closely resembles %1$s but is not its official domain. Such sites are used to steal credentials.
This domain uses encoded characters and may look almost identical to a real site. Check it carefully.
This domain ends in .%1$s; such suffixes are free to register and often used for throwaway fraud sites.
Legitimate sites normally use domain names. A raw IP over an unencrypted connection often indicates a hastily set-up phishing page.
The domain contains an unusually long segment, often used to hide the real destination.
The domain has an unusually deep hierarchy, possibly random subdomains used to evade blocking.
The domain contains many digits and may be an automatically generated throwaway site.
This domain distributes the SilverFox trojan, which steals contacts and SMS messages.
This domain is linked to SilverFox (a remote-access trojan).
